To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) oxidative damage to DNA and proteins is increased in ageing, 2) oxidative stress can accelerate the ageing process and 3) the ability to respond to and repair oxidants can delay ageing.
the production of reactive oxygen species and the response to oxidative stress are intricately connected to life span.
the rate of ageing and longevity are determined by the rate of production and removal of reactive oxygen species (ROS).
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the molecular basis of ageing, and in particular how the ageing process is regulated.
the role of reactive oxygen species in ageing.
the molecular mechanisms of ageing and age-related disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
oxidative stress is not the cause of ageing but that oxidative stress is a consequence of ageing.
oxidative stress is not the only cause of ageing, but that it plays an important role in the process.
oxidative stress and ageing are intimately connected, but the precise nature and extent of the connections remains unclear.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
oxidants and antioxidant systems play a central role in the biology of ageing and life span.
oxidative stress is not a cause of ageing but rather an important consequence of ageing.
the oxidative stress response, and the ability to maintain redox balance and to repair oxidative damage to cellular macromolecules is critical for the maintenance of healthy tissues and longevity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the rate and degree of ageing are not fixed, but are instead modulated by the environment, the genome and the epigenome.
the ability of organisms, from yeast to mice, to cope with oxidative stress is a key determinant of longevity.
oxidative stress, which is the imbalance between oxidants and antioxidants in favour of the former, is a key factor in ageing.
